    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). This month is missing *Nat Mach Intell*. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: JAMA 136, Nature 133, Science 104, Nucleic Acids Res 91, Blood 54, N Engl J Med 50.

## 3. The evidence that moved it








**Cell therapy stopped needing a factory.** Two papers in one month generate CAR
T cells inside the patient: [41851456](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41851456/) (*Nature*) reprograms T
cells in vivo by site-specific engineering, and [41882404](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41882404/)
(*Nat Med*) infuses ESO-T01, a nanobody-directed immune-shielded lentiviral
vector encoding an anti-BCMA CAR, into five heavily pretreated myeloma patients
with no leukapheresis, no ex vivo manufacture and no lymphodepletion. Four of
five responded, three with stringent complete remission, and all four evaluable
responders were MRD-negative by day 60. Read the size and the stopping rule
before the response rate: it is five patients, the trial was stopped early in
2025 with no further enrolment, and every patient had a grade 3 or higher
adverse event. The abstract's own opening sentence places it after existing
clinical experience with in vivo CAR-T generation rather than ahead of it. Ex
vivo manufacturing is the cost, delay and access constraint on the entire
platform, and removing it would change who can be treated more than any receptor
redesign in this corpus — which is why the size of the evidence here matters.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This section carried a paragraph headed "The tumour microbiome was told to
    start over", built on
    [41650974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41650974/) stating that most
    published tumour-microbiome signatures are contamination artifacts that do
    not reproduce. The paper never assesses published signatures. It also used a
    *Cell* paper from two months later as the "replacement", which is an
    argument this briefing cannot make from inside April. Both halves are
    withdrawn and the paragraph below states what the abstract reports.

**The tumour microbiome got a decontamination method, and the map it produced is
narrower than the thread's claim.** [41650974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41650974/) (*Cancer Cell*)
introduces PRISM, a framework for identifying microorganisms in low-biomass
sequencing and stripping contaminants, benchmarked on 230 independent datasets
with known true-positive and contaminant taxa. Applied to 25 cancer types across
TCGA and CPTAC it recovers consistent microbial signatures in gastrointestinal,
head-and-neck and urogenital tumours, and sparse signal elsewhere; in pancreatic
cancer, microbial detection tracks altered host protein glycosylation and greater
smoking exposure. That is a real signal and a usable method. It is carded as a
refutation on `neuro-immune-microbiome-axis` because of the second half: the
thread claims one mechanism network, and a microbial arm confined to sites with
mucosal contact constrains that claim's reach rather than evidencing it. The
mechanism is not in doubt where it exists.

**ctDNA got a clean prospective win.** [41813900](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41813900/)
(*Nature*) validates risk-adaptive therapy guided by dynamic ctDNA prospectively
in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Against a thread whose recorded negatives are about
what happens *after* detection rather than about detection itself, this is the
design that works: a disease with a clean viral marker, and a randomized
structure where ctDNA sets the therapy rather than annotating it.

**Foundation models split cleanly by task type again.** [Evo 2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41781614/)
models and designs genomes across all domains of life, and
[CellVoyager](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41845065/) autonomously analyses single-cell data with a
benchmark across 76 studies. And [41912799](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41912799/) (*Nat Methods*)
co-distils ESM models against each other — each learning from the most confident
predictions of the others — to reach state-of-the-art variant-effect prediction
from raw unaligned sequence alone, without structure, homology or
population-genetics inputs, and then quantifies variant severity against
continuous clinical phenotypes in biobank data. It was carded here as an
ensemble squeezed into a small model, undercutting scale from the inside. The
paper argues something else and says so: it challenges the prevailing view that
sequence-only protein language models are intrinsically limited. Nothing in it
concerns model size, and it is another win on a sequence-to-function task with
hard ground truth.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

The PRISM card above is filed as a refutation on
`neuro-immune-microbiome-axis`, and it is the largest single hit that thread has
taken. Note what it does *not* touch: the neural arm. Two supports this month —
[serotonin and lineage plasticity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41416996/) and
[lymphocyte-intrinsic cholinergic circuits](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41735533/) — are both neural,
neither microbial. The thread is one mechanism network by claim, but its two
arms are not in the same evidentiary state, and the microbial arm is the weaker
one: PRISM finds it at sites with mucosal contact and little of it elsewhere.

Two further supports were counted here and should not have been.
[41677804](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41677804/) and [41785384](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41785384/)
are *Cancer Discovery* research-watch items with no abstract and no named
authors. They restate, respectively, [41650969](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41650969/) (*Cell*,
February) on sensory neurons driving immune exclusion through a dense
extracellular matrix in breast cancer, and [41616781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41616781/) (*Cell*,
March) on sympathetic-epithelial crosstalk positioning tissue-resident memory T
cells in skin. Both primaries are carded on this thread in their own months, so
counting the echoes put those two studies on the thread's supports side twice —
on the thread with the largest supports side in the corpus. Both echoes are now
neutral, and April's neural evidence is the two cards named above.

[41606121](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41606121/) (*Nat Med*) is the exception worth reading: faecal
transplant plus checkpoint blockade where benefit tracks **loss of deleterious
taxa, not donor engraftment**. That inverts the standard model of what FMT does
and is the most actionable microbiome card in the corpus.

### (b) Method credibility

Four cards, and three of them are about reproducibility of the analysis rather
than of the biology. [41903535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41903535/) (*Cell Syst*): identical
single-cell data give materially different clusters and differential expression
across *package versions*. [41775267](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41775267/): gene essentiality calls do
not transfer across genetic backgrounds — every DepMap-derived target list
inherits this. [41998753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41998753/): a recurrent instrument-chemistry
artifact produces false somatic variant calls on two-colour Illumina platforms.

On the model side, [40500472](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40500472/) (*Nat Biotechnol*) is the sharpest:
standard cell-embedding benchmark metrics *reward* embeddings that destroy
biological structure. This is the second of three months in which the metric,
rather than the method, is what fails — see June's
[40739072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40739072/) on silhouette-based integration metrics.
[41922570](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41922570/): protein language model embeddings carry unquantified,
task-dependent uncertainty, so downstream confidence is uncalibrated.
